title: Google Will Pay Homes and Businesses to Use Less Power for Data Centers
excerpt: Google and Voltus will build a 1-gigawatt virtual power plant in PJM, paying participants to cut peak use so new data centre load can connect faster.
body:
• Google and Voltus announced on October 22, 2026 an expanded 1-gigawatt virtual power plant in PJM — ten times their 100-megawatt June deal — funded by Google and run by Voltus through 2040.
  • How it works: Voltus pays homes and businesses to cut or shift power at peak times using smart thermostats, batteries, EVs and industrial adjustments; together those small cuts act like a power plant.
  • PJM serves 67 million people in 13 states and Washington, D.C., and has missed reliability margins as data centre demand surges; the VPP is meant to add capacity faster than building generation.
  • If you live in PJM territory, participation is voluntary and paid — bill savings and cash payments — in exchange for allowing brief, limited adjustments during grid strain events.

Google will pay other people to use less electricity so its data centres can use more. That is the plain version of the deal Google announced with Voltus on October 22: a 1-gigawatt virtual power plant across the PJM grid region, which serves 67 million people across 13 states and Washington, D.C.

The expanded agreement adds 1,070 megawatts to an initial 100-megawatt deal signed in June, according to Utility Dive. Google calls it one of the largest known distributed capacity portfolios deployed by a hyperscaler to date. Voltus expects to ramp to full capacity over three to four years and run the arrangement under contract with Google through 2040.

Demand response, explained

A virtual power plant is not a building. It is a coordinated network of small resources that, acting together, behave like a power plant. In this case, Voltus aggregates flexible capacity from homes, businesses and industrial sites: a smart thermostat nudged up two degrees, a home or factory battery discharging, an electric vehicle pausing its charge, or a production line shifting a process by an hour.

None of those changes matters alone. Thousands together, triggered at the same peak moment, free up a gigawatt — roughly the output of a large conventional plant — without burning fuel or building transmission. When the grid is strained, Voltus offers that combined capacity into PJM's market, and participants receive bill savings and cash payments funded by Google.

Fast Company describes the lived experience: a big-box store automatically adjusts its thermostat, a factory runs part of production on battery, a car in a garage delays charging. In many cases, the company says, occupants may not notice.

"Virtual power plants are the clean, firm resource that we have available today. So this is really our way to assist the grid, especially one like PJM, which is facing capacity shortages."

— Ellen Zuckerman, head of energy market development for North and South America, Google

Why PJM, and why now

PJM is the largest U.S. wholesale power market. Utility Dive reports it has recently fallen short of its reliability margins despite sharply higher capacity auction prices, driven in large part by rising data centre demand. Demand response revenue in PJM jumped 240% from 2024 to 2025, reaching $523.5 million, according to Monitoring Analytics, the grid operator's market monitor.

For Google, the logic is timing. New generation and transmission take years to permit and build. Paying for flexibility that already exists — thermostats, batteries and industrial loads already installed — can be contracted and deployed far faster. Voltus CEO Dana Guernsey has compared such long-term hyperscaler contracts to the power purchase agreements that unlocked financing for wind and solar, a comparison Utility Dive notes industry sources see as a turning point for distributed resources.

Who benefits, and what to watch

Participants are the most direct beneficiaries: Voltus says energy users in PJM can earn substantial demand-response payments, and Google and Voltus both stress direct payments plus lower bills. Non-participants can benefit too if peak shaving puts downward pressure on prices for everyone — a point supported by a Brattle Group report cited by both companies, which also estimates better grid utilisation could save U.S. consumers more than $100 billion over the next decade.

The risks are execution and scale. Voltus has about 8.5 gigawatts under contract across North America and aims for 20 gigawatts by 2030, after raising $225 million earlier this month. Whether a tenfold expansion stays oversubscribed — as Google says the first 100 megawatts quickly were — will determine if this becomes a template other hyperscalers copy across other strained grids.
